newSections.title: A Texas primary document before Medicine Lodge
newSections.text: The 1844 Tehuacana Creek text joins peace provisions with regulated trade, government agents and proposed English-language, Christian and agricultural instruction. Its 22 articles make those different aims visible together. The document lists several Indigenous parties separately; a shared instrument does not merge their identities. References to a line do not themselves establish a precise agreed territorial boundary.

newSections.title: Penateka diplomacy and German settlement
newSections.text: Babcock’s study of the 1847 Meusebach agreement gives Comanche leaders and intermediaries a role alongside the German negotiator. He challenges accounts that credit one man alone and places negotiations within settlement pressures. His interpretation is useful to compare with the primary record; it should not become a claim that every Comanche band accepted the same agreement or that later pressures disappeared.

newSections.title: Remembering code talkers through families and language
newSections.text: In the Nation’s report, Lloyd Heminokeky explains the importance of honoring code talkers through family participation and language-department work. LaNora Parker describes her father Simmons Parker as a teacher of Comanche history and pride. These named accounts connect public remembrance with family learning, without defining every family’s experience or reproducing songs and ceremonial material.
